---
title: "Travel-time matrices"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
```

`travel_time_matrix()` returns, for every origin and destination, how long
the trip takes. This article explains what decides that number, mode by mode,
and which arguments change it. All the code runs on the sample network
bundled with the package:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(peabiru)
data_path <- system.file("extdata/spo", package = "peabiru")
network <- build_network(data_path, n_threads = 2)
points <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "spo_points.csv"))
departure <- as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")
```

## Streets: walking, cycling, driving

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Street routing: a point is linked to the nearest street open to the mode, a search expands directed edges from the origin up to the time limit, and each destination is reached through either end of its own edge. Walking uses walk_speed; cycling uses bike_speed up to max_lts and walks the bike elsewhere; driving uses each edge's speed, turn costs and turn restrictions."}
fig("street-routing.svg")
```

Each point is first *linked* to the street network: to the nearest street
that the mode may use, looking within 300 m and then within 1600 m. A point
with no such street is not routed, and its pairs are missing from the result.
The stretch between the point and the street is walked, whatever the mode.

The search then runs over the streets until the time limit:
`max_trip_duration`, or the mode's own limit (`max_walk_time`,
`max_bike_time`, `max_car_time`) when it is lower. Times are rounded down to
whole minutes, and pairs beyond the limit are left out of the result rather
than returned as `NA`.

```{r}
walk <- travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode = "WALK",
                           n_threads = 2)
nrow(walk) == nrow(points)^2

walk15 <- travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode = "WALK",
                             max_walk_time = 15, n_threads = 2)
nrow(walk15)
range(walk15$travel_time_p50)
```

Cyclists ride at `bike_speed` on streets whose *level of traffic stress*
(LTS, from 1 to 4, derived from the OpenStreetMap tags) is at most `max_lts`.
On more stressful streets they get off and walk the bike, so a cautious
cyclist is slower:

```{r}
lts <- sapply(1:4, function(l) {
  m <- travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode = "BICYCLE",
                          max_lts = l, n_threads = 2)
  mean(m$travel_time_p50)
})
setNames(round(lts, 2), paste0("max_lts = ", 1:4))
```

Cars use each street's speed (its `maxspeed` tag, or a default for its road
class), pay 10 s for a right turn, 30 s for a left turn and 90 s for a U-turn,
and obey turn restrictions.

## Public transport

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "How a public transport travel-time matrix is computed: walk from the origin, RAPTOR over every departure minute of the window (with Monte Carlo draws for frequency-based trips), walk to each destination, then percentiles over the minutes and draws."}
fig("transit-matrix.svg")
```

With `mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT")` a trip is a walk to a stop, up to
`max_rides` vehicles with walking transfers between them, and a walk to the
destination, or simply a walk all the way. The search is repeated for every
minute of `time_window` starting at `departure_datetime`; the matrix reports
`percentiles` of those travel times.

```{r}
ttm <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure,
  time_window = 10,
  percentiles = c(10, 50, 90),
  seed = 42,
  n_threads = 2
)
head(ttm)
```

### Frequency-based feeds and `seed`

When a feed gives frequencies (a bus every 10 minutes) instead of timetables,
the exact departure times are unknown. Each departure minute is then
simulated `draws_per_minute` times with random offsets, so the percentiles
also reflect the uncertainty of the schedule. The draws come from a random
number generator seeded by `seed` and the origin's coordinates: with a seed
the result is reproducible; without one it changes from run to run.

```{r}
again <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, percentiles = c(10, 50, 90),
  seed = 42, n_threads = 2
)
identical(ttm, again)

other <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, percentiles = c(10, 50, 90),
  seed = 7, n_threads = 2
)
mean(other$travel_time_p50 != ttm$travel_time_p50)
```

### The time window

A single departure minute still varies with a frequency-based feed (the
draws), but a wider window also averages over when you leave:

```{r}
spread <- function(m) mean(m$travel_time_p90 - m$travel_time_p10)
tw1 <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, time_window = 1,
  percentiles = c(10, 50, 90), seed = 42, n_threads = 2
)
c(time_window_1 = spread(tw1), time_window_10 = spread(ttm))
```

### Walking limits

`max_walk_time` limits each walk (the access walk, each transfer and the
egress walk) and also the walk-only option; transfers are never longer than
1 km. Pairs that need more walking than allowed disappear from the result:

```{r}
short_walks <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, max_walk_time = 5,
  seed = 42, n_threads = 2
)
c(default = nrow(ttm), max_walk_time_5 = nrow(short_walks))
```

## Threads

`n_threads` (all cores by default) spreads the origins over threads. The
result does not depend on it.

```{r}
one <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure, percentiles = c(10, 50, 90),
  seed = 42, n_threads = 1
)
identical(one, ttm)
```

## Stopping a long call

An interrupt (Esc, or Ctrl-C in a terminal) stops any of the routing
functions within a few tenths of a second and returns to the prompt, with
no partial result. `setTimeLimit()` works too, and `tryCatch(interrupt = )`
sees the interrupt as it would for R code. `build_network()` cannot be
interrupted.
